summary: Philipp Schmid addresses the gap between widespread adoption of AI agent skills and the near-total absence of evaluations. Skill Bench indexed over 50,000 skills and found almost none had evaluations. This matters because agents are non-deterministic: when a task fails, you cannot distinguish a bad skill from a task that exceeds model capability. Schmid draws a critical distinction between agents developers use (coding agents like Cursor, Claude Code) and agents built for consumers. Developers have context about skills and notice when one fails to trigger; end users do not, so consumer-facing agents depend entirely on model-triggered skills with strong descriptions. A skill is fundamentally a folder with a skills.md file plus assets, built on progressive disclosure: a title and description always in context, a body with more detail read on demand, and reference files for deep exploration. Schmid distinguishes capability skills (temporary, teaching models new abilities that may be retired as models improve) from preference skills (durable, encoding team-specific workflows). Skillsbench 1.1 data shows skills improve performance by roughly 15% across about 100 coding and productivity tasks. Human-written skills outperform AI-generated ones, which can hurt performance. Schmid then presents a practical example: a skill for the Gemini Interactions API, created because the API was released after Gemini's last training. The team built 117 test cases from real user data and synthetic cases, achieving nearly 90% performance for generating valid API code with the latest models. The eval harness was lightweight—a JSON file with prompts, language, should-trigger flags, and expected checks, plus a Python script running a coding agent. Most assertions were regex-based (checking SDK, model, methods, old patterns), which are cheap to run. LLM-as-judge with a rubric handles complex traces. At Google DeepMind, evals run alongside every skill on every change, and changes are blocked unless they improve test cases. Ten best practices follow: skill descriptions are critical (50% of failures from incorrect triggering), write directives not passive information, include negative tests, start small with 10-20 samples, test outcomes not paths, use isolated runs to prevent agents cheating by finding context elsewhere, run 3-6 trials per case for reliability, test across different harnesses since agent behavior varies, keep evals when retiring skills to detect degradation and enable reintroduction, and run ablation tests with and without the skill loaded.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: Why skills need evals
sections.summary: Schmid opens by asking the audience to raise hands: most use coding agents with skills, but almost none have evals for those skills. He introduces Skill Bench as a benchmark that indexed over 50,000 skills and found almost none were tested.

sections.title: The problem: non-deterministic agents and untested skills
sections.summary: Schmid explains that agents are non-deterministic, making it hard to know if a task fails because the skill is bad or because the task is too challenging for the model. Most skills are AI-written and not really tested.

sections.title: Agents we use vs. agents we build
sections.summary: Schmid distinguishes agents developers use (Cursor, Claude Code) where they have skill context and notice missed triggers, from consumer-facing agents where users have no idea what skills are and won't invoke them by name.

sections.title: Defining a skill and progressive disclosure
sections.summary: A skill is a folder with a skills.md file plus assets. Progressive disclosure means the title and description are always in context, the skill body provides more detail on demand, and reference files allow deep exploration.

sections.title: Capability skills vs. preference skills
sections.summary: Capability skills teach models things they cannot yet do consistently and are temporary—evals tell when to retire them. Preference skills encode company-specific workflows and styles, are more durable, and must be protected with evals.

sections.title: Do skills work? Skillsbench data
sections.summary: Skillsbench 1.1 shows skills improve performance by roughly 15% across about 100 tasks. Human-written skills are best; AI-generated skills can hurt performance. Skills.md files should stay below 500 lines.

sections.title: Model-triggered vs. user-invoked skills
sections.summary: Model-triggered skills rely on context and description for the model to decide usage. User-invoked skills are powerful for workflow tasks like creating PRs. Consumer-facing agents only use model-invoked skills, which is the focus for evals.

sections.title: Best practices for writing skills
sections.summary: Eight tips: write descriptions with why, how, and when; use directives not essays; keep skills lean and layered with references; set goals and constraints not rigid steps (use scripts for fixed workflows); include negative cases; test early with 10-20 prompts including production traces; remove no-ops; and know when to retire skills as models and environments evolve.

sections.title: Retiring skills and practical example: Gemini Interactions API
sections.summary: Skills can be retired when the model achieves performance without triggering them, saving token cost and maintenance. Schmid presents a practical example: a skill for the Gemini Interactions API, released after Gemini's last training, so the model had no knowledge of it. The team created 117 test cases from real user data and synthetic cases, improving performance up to almost 90% for generating valid interactions API code with the latest models.

sections.title: Building a lightweight eval harness
sections.summary: The eval harness needs only two assets: a JSON file with test cases (prompt, language, should-trigger flag, expected checks) and a Python script running a coding agent (Gemini CLI). Most assertions are regex-based—checking correct SDK, model, methods, and old patterns—which are cheap to run and easy to update when new models release. LLM-as-judge with a rubric handles complex traces requiring analysis of full steps.

sections.title: How Google DeepMind evaluates skills
sections.summary: At Google DeepMind, evals accompany every skill internally. Each test has multiple cases with prompts, run in isolated workspaces with optional additional files and startup commands. Script evals use regex to inspect traces for triggered skills and commands run. LLM-as-judge checks expectations. Evals run on every skill diff; changes are blocked unless they improve test cases, enforcing regression testing.

sections.title: Top 10 best practices summary
sections.summary: Ten practices: skill descriptions are critical (50% of failures from incorrect triggering); write directives not passive information; include negative tests; start small with 10-20 samples; test outcomes not paths; use isolated runs to prevent cheating; run 3-6 trials per case for reliability; test across different harnesses since behavior varies; keep evals after retiring skills to detect degradation; and create evals to know when to retire skills.

sections.title: Homework: Start testing your skills
sections.summary: Schmid assigns homework: pick your most used skill, write five test prompts, build a simple eval harness (JSON/YAML plus Python script), remove no-ops to save cost, reference Matt's writing great skills guide on GitHub, and run ablation tests with and without the skill loaded to determine if it is truly helpful.
